basis: Written from the published specification and established practice in the field; no new sources were read. Unreviewed.

distinguishingFeatures: A taxon concept according to a stated authority, not the bare scientific name.
The same name can denote different circumscriptions in different sources, and the model keeps them apart.
Concept relations such as congruent, includes or overlaps link concepts across classifications.
Organisms, specimens and occurrences are separate records that reference a taxon.

may: Resolve a name to candidate taxon concepts with their authorities.
Report concept relations and mappings between checklists.
Suggest an identification with stated uncertainty.
Record evidence references for a placement.
mustNot: Treat a name string match as proof that two concepts are the same.
Publish a new name or nomenclatural act.
Disclose precise locations of threatened taxa where data are sensitive.
Give certain identifications of toxic or dangerous species from images alone.
requiresHuman: Taxonomic revisions and acceptance decisions in a checklist.
Identifications used for medical, legal or biosecurity decisions.

considerations: Precise locations of rare species can be used by poachers and collectors.
Misidentifying poisonous or invasive species can harm people and ecosystems.
Indigenous and local names and knowledge deserve credit and consent.

properties.reason: A taxon is an abstract classification concept; organisms and specimens carry the physical properties.

items: A taxon concept is recognised by a scientific name plus the according-to source and a diagnosis.
Organisms of a taxon are confused with look-alike species, hybrids and different life stages.
Wrong identification of venomous, poisonous or invasive organisms.
Merging distinct concepts and losing conservation status.
Leak of sensitive locations of threatened species.
International Codes of Nomenclature (ICZN, ICN, ICNP).
